result.summary: Pausanias describes statues of the Muses and of poets and musicians at the grove of the Muses on Helicon. He then digresses on Orpheus, giving rival accounts of his death and tomb, including the tale of Libethra's destruction by the river Sus, and ends with a note on the Hymns of Orpheus.

scenes.title: Statues on Helicon
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists statues of the Muses, gods, poets and musicians at Helicon, noting Sulla's plundered Dionysus and errors in some portraits.

scenes.title: Orpheus and his deaths
scenes.summary: Pausanias doubts the myths about Orpheus but praises his poetry and rites, and reports varying accounts of his death, including by Thracian women.

scenes.title: Orpheus's tomb at Dium
scenes.summary: The Macedonians of Pieria say Orpheus was slain near Dium and show his urn; the river Helicon vanishes underground to avoid cleansing his killers.

scenes.title: Libethra destroyed by Sus
scenes.summary: An oracle warned that Libethra would fall when the Sun saw Orpheus's bones. A sleeping shepherd's singing drew a crowd that broke the urn, and the river Sus flooded the city.
scenes.stakes: The whole city of Libethra and its people face destruction.

scenes.title: The Hymns of Orpheus
scenes.summary: Pausanias remarks that the Hymns of Orpheus are few and short, chanted by the Lycomidæ, and rank next to Homer's.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias quotes a Greek proverb about worshipping with other people's incense.
Pausanias rationalizes the Orpheus myth, doubting the animals and descent to Hades.

analysis.text: Pausanias weighs local traditions critically, noting rival claims about Orpheus's death and tomb while accepting his historical importance.
The passage shows Roman plunder of Greek art, as Sulla took a statue from Orchomenus, and the Greek habit of sacred sites competing for relics.

legacy.text: The tale of Orpheus's death and tomb fed later Orphic literature and the long tradition of Orpheus as the archetypal poet.

fun_facts.text: The oracle plays on the name Sus, which means boar in Greek, as well as naming the river.

language_notes.text: A Greek proverb for being pious or generous at someone else's expense; Sulla dedicated plunder as though it were his own gift.
Pindar's prelude, a lost poem, apparently praised the piper Sacadas's great music; the sculptor mistook it as describing a small man.
Laurel wand: the staff of laurel which Hesiod says the Muses gave him, used by rhapsodes when reciting, instead of a harp.
Pausanias distinguishes Calliope from the daughter of Pierus, a different Muse-named mother of Orpheus in another tradition; he prefers the latter.
Aornus in Thesprotia was the site of an oracle of the dead (necromanteion), where souls could be consulted.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet (about 180 metres), so 20 stades is a little over two miles.
Blood-guiltiness means the ritual pollution incurred by shedding blood, which in Greek belief required purification by water.
The oracle's "Sus" is the Greek word for boar. Its double sense, animal or river, is the riddle on which the story turns.
"The Sun did see the remains" fulfils the oracle literally: the broken urn exposes the bones to daylight.
The Lycomidæ were an Athenian priestly clan who kept a hereditary cult at Phlya and sang Orphic hymns in their rites.

context_notes.text: Sulla, the Roman general, sacked Greek sanctuaries in the 80s BC during the Mithridatic War, taking statues from Orchomenus, home of the Minyans.
Thamyris was a legendary Thracian singer blinded by the Muses for boasting; Arion was a poet said to have been rescued by a dolphin.
Telete personifies initiation into mystic rites, fitting Orpheus's association with mysteries.
Orpheus, the legendary Thracian singer, was said to have been killed by women, often Thracian Bacchantes, angered at him. Dium lay at the foot of Mount Olympus.
Pausanias here gives a second tradition, heard from locals at Larissa in Thessaly. Libethra was a town near Olympus associated with the Muses and Orpheus.
The Mysteries were secret religious rites open only to initiates. Orphic poetry was closely tied to such cults.

literary_notes.text: The popular saying neatly condemns Sulla's hypocrisy in a witty, compact way.
Pausanias speaks as a skeptical, rationalizing observer, separating popular belief from what he judges credible.
The story explains a custom, men fighting drunk, by an origin legend, though Pausanias presents it only as hearsay.
The sweet-singing nightingales at the tomb offer a gentle, poignant close after violent accounts of the singer's death.
The river is treated as a moral agent, hiding itself underground to refuse purification to the murderers.
The Libethrians dismiss the oracle by thinking of a boar, yet the doom comes from a river of that name.
The shepherd's sleeping song, with the tomb nearby, hints that Orpheus's music will again have power and set the oracle's fulfilment in motion.
The long sweeping list of what was destroyed conveys total, impersonal catastrophe, and it closes the oracle's prophecy with grim finality.
